sections.title: Basic Concept of Statement and Argument
sections.content: In Statement and Argument questions, a statement is given followed by several arguments. The candidate must identify which argument is strong and which is weak. Step 1: Understand the main issue in the statement. Step 2: Read each argument separately. Step 3: Check whether the argument is directly related to the statement. Step 4: Evaluate the logical strength of the argument.

sections.title: Characteristics of Strong Arguments
sections.content: A strong argument is based on facts, practical experience, or logical reasoning. Step 1: Check whether the argument is factual. Step 2: Determine whether it is directly related to the statement. Step 3: See whether it is based on practical reasoning or common truth. Step 4: Check whether it helps in making a decision. Example: If the statement is 'Should plastic bags be banned in the city?' the argument 'Yes, because plastic harms the environment' is considered strong.

sections.title: Identifying Weak Arguments
sections.content: A weak argument is based on personal opinion, emotional appeal, or unclear reasoning. Step 1: Check whether the argument is merely an opinion. Step 2: See whether it lacks a solid reason. Step 3: Determine whether it is not directly related to the statement. Step 4: Check whether it is based only on comparison or imitation. Example: 'Yes, because other countries also do this' may be a weak argument.

sections.title: Emotional vs Logical Arguments
sections.content: Sometimes an argument may sound emotionally convincing but is logically weak. Step 1: Identify emotional words. Step 2: Check whether any factual reason is given. Step 3: Determine whether the argument is truly related to the problem. Step 4: Do not make decisions based only on emotions.

sections.title: Direct Relevance Check
sections.content: A strong argument is always connected to the main issue in the statement. Step 1: Identify the main topic of the statement. Step 2: Look for reasons in the argument that relate to the same topic. Step 3: If the argument moves away from the topic, it is likely weak.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Treating emotional appeal as a strong argument. 2. Not checking whether the argument relates to the statement. 3. Treating personal opinion as fact. 4. Assuming popularity is a valid argument.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: A strong argument is based on facts, experience, and logical reasoning. A weak argument is usually based on opinion, emotion, or vague reasons. Always evaluate the relevance and strength of the argument in relation to the statement.

tricks.title: Fact Check Method
tricks.explanation: If the argument is based on a fact or a real reason, it is often strong.
tricks.example: Plastic ban should be implemented because plastic harms the environment.

tricks.title: Opinion Trap
tricks.explanation: If the argument is based on statements like 'I think' or 'people say', it may be weak.
tricks.example: Yes, because many people like this idea.

tricks.title: Direct Link Rule
tricks.explanation: The argument must be directly related to the statement.
tricks.example: School uniforms should be mandatory because they promote discipline.

tricks.title: Emotion vs Logic Test
tricks.explanation: If the argument only creates emotion but does not give a reason, it is weak.
tricks.example: Yes, because it would make people very happy.

tricks.title: Copying Other Countries Trap
tricks.explanation: Just because other countries follow something does not make it a strong argument.
tricks.example: Yes, because the US follows this rule.

tricks.title: Practicality Check
tricks.explanation: If the argument shows a practical outcome, it may be strong.
tricks.example: Ban on plastic will reduce pollution.

tricks.title: Identify Irrelevant Argument
tricks.explanation: If the argument talks about something unrelated to the statement, it is weak.
tricks.example: Yes, because the city has many parks.

tricks.title: Universal Truth Rule
tricks.explanation: If the argument is based on a general truth or established fact, it is strong.
